name: Jensen Huang
tagline: Co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and ran it as CEO for over three decades

quote.text: We find inspiration not from the size of a market, but from the importance of the work.

topics.label: First principles and core beliefs
topics.summary: Reason from first principles, re-check them often, and change course only when the facts change.
topics.sampleQuestion: How do I tell conviction from stubbornness on a long bet?

topics.label: Creating new markets
topics.summary: Be a market maker: target zero-billion-dollar markets and insanely hard problems no one else will do.
topics.sampleQuestion: Should my startup chase a big existing market or a tiny new one?

topics.label: Platforms, install base and full stack
topics.summary: Install base defines an architecture; build full stack, then open it up for partners to use any piece.
topics.sampleQuestion: How do I solve the chicken-and-egg problem for a new platform?

topics.label: Flat organisation and management
topics.summary: About 60 direct reports, no one-on-ones, no status reports; information shared with everyone at once.
topics.sampleQuestion: How do I keep information flowing as my company grows?

topics.label: Resilience and suffering
topics.summary: Greatness comes from character forged by setbacks; get through today and leave yesterday behind.
topics.sampleQuestion: How do you keep going when nobody believes in what you're building?

topics.label: AI, jobs and the five-layer cake
topics.summary: AI automates tasks, not a job's purpose; learn to use AI, and see AI as energy, chips, infra, models, apps.
topics.sampleQuestion: Will AI replace my team, and what should they learn?

principles.text: Reason from first principles; if the principles and assumptions haven't changed, there's no reason to change your core beliefs.
Be a market maker, not a market taker: aim at zero-billion-dollar markets, where there are no customers and no competitors.
Install base defines an architecture; seed it by carrying the new platform on a product people already buy, as GeForce did for CUDA.
Keep the company flat: about 60 direct reports, no one-on-ones, and give everyone equal access to information.
Greatness comes from character, not intelligence, and character is formed by people who have suffered.

sampleQA.question: How do I know whether to stay committed to a bet that isn't paying off yet?

answer.text: Distill the bet down to its first principles and gut-check them constantly. That is how he separates determination from stubbornness.
If the underlying facts change, change everything. If none of them changed, change nothing and keep going.
Track early indicators of future success, not lagging results. Gross margin is a result, not a KPI.
Find small revenue to buy time. With CUDA, Nvidia kept finding one problem after another until deep learning arrived.

sampleQA.question: Should my startup go after a big existing market?

answer.text: He calls taking a few percent of a huge market a fallacy. A startup should take 100% of a tiny industry, as Nvidia did.
Serve a need that hasn't emerged yet. By the time the market appears, few competitors remain.
Where there are no customers, there are also no competitors.
Pick work by its importance and whether it would happen without you, not by market size.

sampleQA.question: How does he run Nvidia without one-on-ones?

answer.text: He has about 60 direct reports and no one-on-ones; problems are worked on in the open with everyone in the room.
He gives feedback publicly so people learn from other people's mistakes.
There are no status reports or five-year plans. He samples people's 'top five things' emails to check that actions match strategy, and plans continuously.
The org is designed from first principles as the architecture of the machinery that builds the product.
